document.title: Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025

record.title: Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025
record.summary: A ClickHouse permissions change caused a query used to generate Cloudflare's Bot Management feature file to return duplicate rows, doubling the file's size. This exceeded a hardcoded feature limit in the Bot Management module, causing the core proxy (FL2) to panic and return HTTP 5xx errors across the network, while FL proxy customers got bot scores of zero. The team initially suspected a DDoS attack before identifying and rolling back the bad configuration file, restoring most traffic by 14:30 and fully resolving remaining issues by 17:06.

trigger.label: config_change
trigger.quote: Database access control change deployed.
trigger.description: A change to ClickHouse database permissions deployed at 11:05 UTC made underlying table metadata explicitly visible, causing a query to return duplicate rows.

change_at.quote: Database access control change deployed.

mechanism.label: limit_violation
mechanism.quote: When the bad file with more than 200 features was propagated to our servers, this limit was hit — resulting in the system panicking.
mechanism.description: The doubled feature file exceeded the Bot Management module's hardcoded 200-feature limit, causing an unhandled Rust panic and 5xx errors.

detected_at.quote: The first automated test detected the issue at 11:31

mitigations.text: Workers KV and Cloudflare Access bypass implemented to fall back to a prior version of the core proxy
Stopped creation and propagation of new Bot Management configuration files
Rolled back Bot Management configuration file to a last-known-good version and deployed globally
Scaled control plane concurrency to restore dashboard availability

resolved_at.quote: All services resolved. Impact ends.

blast_radius.qualitative: Cloudflare's worst outage since 2019, causing the majority of core traffic to stop flowing through the network.

impact_start.quote: Deployment reaches customer environments, first errors observed on customer HTTP traffic.

mitigated_at.quote: Main impact resolved. Downstream impacted services started observing reduced errors.

remediations.text: Hardening ingestion of Cloudflare-generated configuration files in the same way we would for user-generated input
Enabling more global kill switches for features
Eliminating the ability for core dumps or other error reports to overwhelm system resources
Reviewing failure modes for error conditions across all core proxy modules

record.detection_quote: The first automated test detected the issue at 11:31 and manual investigation started at 11:32.

contributing_factors.text: An assumption that the metadata query would only return columns from the default database was invalidated once explicit grants were rolled out.
Debugging and observability systems consumed large amounts of CPU while enhancing uncaught errors, increasing latency.
The status page coincidentally went down, misleading the team into suspecting an attack.

record.title: Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025
record.summary: On 18 November 2025, a permissions change to a ClickHouse database cluster caused a query used to generate Cloudflare's Bot Management feature file to return duplicate rows, doubling the file's size. When the oversized file propagated across Cloudflare's network, a hardcoded feature-count limit in the Bot Management module was exceeded, causing the core proxy (FL2) to panic and return HTTP 5xx errors, with FL customers instead receiving invalid all-zero bot scores. The team initially suspected a DDoS attack due to fluctuating good/bad file generation and a coincidental outage of Cloudflare's independently-hosted status page, before identifying the root cause and rolling back to a known-good configuration file, restoring most traffic by 14:30 UTC and fully resolving remaining issues by 17:06 UTC.

contributing_factors.text: Bad data was only generated if the query ran on a part of the ClickHouse cluster which had been updated, so every five minutes there was a chance of good or bad configuration files being generated, causing confusing intermittent recovery and failure that delayed diagnosis.

document.title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31

record.title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31
record.summary: On January 31, 2017, GitLab.com experienced a major outage after an engineer, attempting to rebuild a PostgreSQL secondary that had fallen behind on replication, accidentally ran a data directory wipe command on the primary database server instead of the secondary. Approximately 300GB of production data was removed. Recovery was further complicated because pg_dump backups had been silently failing for months and Azure disk snapshots were not enabled, forcing engineers to restore from a 6-hour-old LVM staging snapshot, resulting in about 18 hours of downtime and permanent loss of roughly 6 hours of data.

trigger.label: manual_command
trigger.quote: Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary. Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead.
trigger.description: An engineer, intending to wipe the PostgreSQL data directory on the secondary to rebuild replication, ran the command against the primary database instead.

change_at.quote: ± 23:00 UTC: Due to the increased load, our PostgreSQL secondary's replication process started to lag behind.

mechanism.label: accidental_data_deletion
mechanism.quote: at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.
mechanism.description: The engineer's command wiped the PostgreSQL data directory on the primary production database, removing about 300GB of data.

detected_at.quote: ± 23:30 UTC: one of the engineers thinks that perhaps pg_basebackup created some files...

mitigations.text: Restored GitLab.com database using a 6-hour-old LVM staging snapshot instead of the ~24-hour-old alternative.
Copied staging data directory to production over ~18 hours, then restored webhooks via a separate staging database dump.
Incremented all database sequences by 100,000 to avoid ID reuse.
Gradually re-enabled GitLab.com service.
Ran a procedure to restore basic project data from Git repositories stored on NFS for projects created after 17:20 UTC.

resolved_at.quote: Around 18:00 UTC we finished the final restoration procedures such as restoring the webhooks and confirming everything was operating as expected.

blast_radius.qualitative: GitLab.com was unavailable for many hours, and some production data was permanently lost.

quantitative.quote: roughly 5,000 projects
5,000 comments
700 new user accounts
GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours.
around 300 GB of data had already been removed
with a peak viewer count of around 5000

impact_start.quote: ± 17:20 UTC: prior to starting this work, our engineer took an LVM snapshot of the production database

mitigated_at.quote: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC we managed to restore the GitLab.com database without webhooks.

remediations.text: Set up Prometheus monitoring for backups.
Set PostgreSQL's max_connections to a sane value.
Investigate point-in-time recovery and continuous archiving for PostgreSQL.
Enable hourly LVM snapshots of production databases.
Enable Azure disk snapshots of production databases.
Move staging to the ARM environment.
Recover production replica(s) and set up multiple secondaries with load balancing.
Automate testing of recovering PostgreSQL database backups.
Improve PostgreSQL replication documentation/runbooks.
Investigate pgbarman and WAL-E for backups and replication.
Assign an owner for data durability.
Set up a public backup monitoring dashboard.
Improve abuse reporting and response system to prevent accidental account deletions.
Build tooling for developers to test database migrations on staging.

record.detection_quote: The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

contributing_factors.text: A spike in database load from spam and an errant account-deletion background job caused replication to the secondary to lag and fail.
pg_dump backups had been silently failing for months due to a PostgreSQL version mismatch (9.2 vs 9.6).
Failure notification emails were rejected because DMARC was not enabled, so nobody knew backups were failing.
Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers because other backup procedures were assumed sufficient.
Replication runbooks did not clearly document normal pg_basebackup wait behavior, contributing to confusion during the incident.

document.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region

record.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region
record.summary: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management system caused a DNS Enactor to overwrite a newer DNS plan with a much older one, which was then deleted by cleanup automation, removing all IP addresses for the regional DynamoDB endpoint. This caused widespread DynamoDB connection failures, which cascaded into EC2 instance launch failures (via DWFM lease congestive collapse), Network Load Balancer health check failures, and impacts to numerous dependent AWS services (Lambda, Connect, STS, IAM, Redshift, Support Console, etc.). Recovery required manual operator intervention on DynamoDB DNS state, followed by staged recovery of EC2, NLB, and dependent services over the following hours.

mechanism.label: race_condition
mechanism.quote: The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system that resulted in an incorrect empty DNS record for the service’s regional endpoint
mechanism.description: A race condition between two independent DNS Enactor instances caused an older DNS plan to overwrite a newer one, which was then deleted by cleanup automation, removing all DNS records for the DynamoDB regional endpoint.

detected_at.quote: By 12:38 AM on October 20, our engineers had identified DynamoDB’s DNS state as the source of the outage.

mitigations.text: Manual operator intervention to correct the inconsistent DynamoDB DNS state.
Engineers throttled incoming work and began selective restarts of DWFM hosts.
Engineers disabled automatic health check failovers for NLB.
Engineers relaxed EC2 request throttles as systems stabilized.
Throttled Lambda Event Source Mappings and asynchronous invocations to prioritize latency-sensitive synchronous invocations.

resolved_at.quote: the event started at 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 and ended at 2:20 PM PDT on October 20

blast_radius.qualitative: Widespread impact across DynamoDB, EC2, NLB, and numerous dependent AWS services in us-east-1, with some effects reaching other regions.

impact_start.quote: When this issue occurred at 11:48 PM PDT

mitigated_at.quote: By 2:25 AM, all DNS information was restored, and all global tables replicas were fully caught up by 2:32 AM.

remediations.text: Disabled the DynamoDB DNS Planner and DNS Enactor automation worldwide.
Will fix the race condition scenario and add additional protections to prevent application of incorrect DNS plans before re-enabling automation.
Adding a velocity control mechanism to limit capacity an NLB can remove during health check failure AZ failover.
Building an additional test suite to exercise the DWFM recovery workflow to identify future regressions.

document.title: 2023-03-08 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue affecting multiple regions | Datadog

record.title: 2023-03-08 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue affecting multiple regions | Datadog
record.summary: On March 8, 2023, an automatic security update to systemd was applied to VMs across five Datadog regions, causing systemd-networkd to forcibly delete CNI-managed routes upon restart, taking affected nodes offline. This caused a global outage affecting all services across US1, EU1, US3, US4, and US5, with users unable to access the platform, monitors unavailable, and data ingestion impacted. Datadog restored web access within hours, declared services operational region by region over the following days, and fully resolved the incident (including historical data backfill) on March 10.

mechanism.quote: systemd-networkd forcibly deleted the routes managed by the Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin (Cilium)
mechanism.description: systemd-networkd forcibly deleted routes managed by the Cilium CNI plugin upon restart, causing affected nodes to go offline.

detected_at.quote: We were first alerted to the issue by our internal monitoring, three minutes after the trigger

mitigations.text: Focused initial efforts on restoring normal ingestion and processing for real-time telemetry data
Switched recovery efforts to historical data once real-time data was usable

Recovered compute capacity per region, scaling beyond normal levels

resolved_at.quote: The incident was fully resolved on March 10, 2023, at 06:25 UTC once we had backfilled historical data.

Quorum-based metadata stores degraded more severely under mass node loss than statically sharded data stores.

document.title: October 21 post-incident analysis

record.title: October 21 post-incident analysis
record.summary: A 43-second network partition during routine maintenance replacing failing 100G optical equipment caused Orchestrator to fail over MySQL primaries from GitHub's US East Coast data center to the US West Coast. This produced unreplicated writes on both coasts, preventing a safe failback and requiring restoration from backups, resulting in 24 hours 11 minutes of degraded service including stale/inconsistent data, paused webhooks, and paused GitHub Pages builds. Data integrity was ultimately preserved, though a few seconds of writes required manual reconciliation.

trigger.label: infrastructure_maintenance
trigger.quote: routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment resulted in the loss of connectivity between our US East Coast network hub and our primary US East Coast data center
trigger.description: Routine maintenance replacing failing 100G optical equipment caused a 43-second loss of connectivity between the East Coast network hub and data center, triggering Orchestrator failover.

change_at.quote: At 22:52 UTC on October 21, routine maintenance work to replace failing 100G optical equipment resulted in the loss of connectivity

mechanism.label: unsafe_failover
mechanism.quote: It’s possible for Orchestrator to implement topologies that applications are unable to support, therefore care must be taken to align Orchestrator’s configuration with application-level expectations.
mechanism.description: Orchestrator failed over MySQL primaries to the West Coast during a brief network partition, a topology the application tier could not safely support, leading to unreplicated writes on both sides and inability to fail back safely.

detected_at.quote: Our internal monitoring systems began generating alerts indicating that our systems were experiencing numerous faults.

mitigations.text: Manually locked internal deployment tooling to prevent additional changes.
Paused webhook delivery and GitHub Pages builds to prioritize data integrity.
Restored affected MySQL clusters from backups and synchronized replicas between sites.
Provisioned additional MySQL read replicas in US East Coast public cloud to spread read load.
Conducted a failover back to the original East Coast topology once replicas were in sync.
Paused webhook processing after discovering dropped payloads and increased the TTL.

resolved_at.quote: All pending webhooks and Pages builds had been processed and the integrity and proper operation of all systems had been confirmed. The site status was updated to green.

record.title: Channel File 291 Incident Root Cause Analysis
record.summary: On July 19, 2024, CrowdStrike deployed new IPC Template Instances via Channel File 291, one of which used a non-wildcard matching criterion for a 21st input field. A pre-existing mismatch between the 21 inputs expected by the Template Type definition and the 20 actually supplied by sensor code, combined with a latent out-of-bounds read in the Content Interpreter, caused sensors receiving this content to crash when evaluating the new criteria. record.title: Incident details
record.summary: On June 12, 2025, a policy change with unintended blank fields was inserted into Service Control's regional Spanner tables and replicated globally within seconds. This exercised a code path (added May 29, 2025) with an unhandled null pointer, crashing Service Control binaries globally and causing widespread 503 errors across Google Cloud and Workspace products. Engineers deployed a red-button to disable the offending policy path, restoring most regions within ~40 minutes, but us-central1 suffered a herd effect overloading its Spanner table, taking up to 2h40m to fully resolve.

trigger.label: config_change
trigger.quote: a policy change was inserted into the regional Spanner tables that Service Control uses for policies. ... This policy data contained unintended blank fields.
trigger.description: An automated policy update containing unintended blank fields was inserted into Service Control's regional Spanner tables and replicated globally.

change_at.quote: a policy change was inserted into the regional Spanner tables

mechanism.label: null_pointer_failure
mechanism.quote: Without the appropriate error handling, the null pointer caused the binary to crash.
mechanism.description: Blank fields in the replicated policy data hit an unhandled null pointer in Service Control's new quota-check code path, crashing binaries into a crash loop globally.

detected_at.quote: Within 2 minutes, our Site Reliability Engineering team was triaging the incident.

mitigations.text: Deployed a red-button to disable the offending policy serving path.
Bypassed the offending quota check to allow recovery in most regions.
Throttled task creation and routed traffic to multi-regional databases in us-central1 to reduce load.
Froze all changes to the Service Control stack and manual policy pushes.

document.title: Slack’s Incident on 2-22-22

record.title: Slack’s Incident on 2-22-22
record.summary: On February 22, 2022, Slack experienced a major incident where users could not connect due to overload in a Vitess keyspace holding channel membership data. A Consul agent upgrade rollout caused memcached nodes to cycle out and back in, emptying caches, which combined with an inefficient scatter query to overwhelm the database. Slack mitigated by throttling client boot requests and later fixed the query to avoid full-shard scans, restoring service.

trigger.label: infrastructure_maintenance
trigger.quote: The PBR step on February 22 updated Consul on 25% of the fleet.
trigger.description: A percentage-based rollout upgrading and restarting the Consul agent fleet caused memcached nodes to cycle out and back in, emptying caches.

mechanism.label: cascading_overload
mechanism.quote: we hit a tipping point and entered a cascading failure scenario as we hit peak traffic for the day
mechanism.description: Cache churn from Consul agent restarts combined with an inefficient scatter query caused database load to spike, entering a self-reinforcing cascading failure state.

detected_at.quote: Just after 6 a.m. Pacific Time, a number of things happened almost simultaneously

mitigations.text: Applied a restrictive throttle to client boot requests to reduce database load.
Paused the Consul agent restart operation.
Modified the problematic scatter query to read only missing data and to read from replicas.
Slowly increased client boot rate limit back to normal levels.

blast_radius.qualitative: Many users unable to connect to Slack, including internal users.

impact_start.quote: Just after 6 a.m. Pacific Time, a number of things happened almost simultaneously

remediations.text: Changed the process for performing Consul rollouts to avoid triggering this failure mode again.
Rolling out changes to the Mcrib control loop to avoid cascading failure from network partitions.
Modified the problematic scatter query to read from a table sharded by channel.
Analyzing other database queries fronted by the cache tier for similar scatter query risks.
Exploring longer-term projects to increase resilience of the caching tier.

record.detection_quote: we began to receive user tickets about problems connecting to Slack, some internal users experienced problems using Slack, and a number of our engineering teams received pages or alerts about problems

contributing_factors.text: An inefficient scatter query required querying every shard on any cache miss for GDM membership data.
Client retries with backoff still contributed additional load during the overload.
Mcrib's efficiency at detecting downed memcached instances increased churn in the cache tier, worsening the incident.

record.title: Slack’s Incident on 2-22-22
record.summary: On February 22, 2022, a Consul agent upgrade rollout caused sequential restarts of memcached nodes, which Slack's Mcrib control plane replaced with empty cache nodes, driving down cache hit rates. Because an inefficient 'scatter query' for Group Direct Message membership had to query every shard of a user-sharded Vitess keyspace on any cache miss, the resulting cache misses overwhelmed the database, triggering a cascading failure that made client boot (and thus login) fail for many users. Slack mitigated the incident by throttling client boot requests, pausing the Consul rollout, and modifying the query to avoid full-shard scans and to use replicas, eventually restoring cache hit rates and normal service.

trigger.label: infrastructure_maintenance
trigger.quote: In the lead-up to this incident, we had been performing maintenance on our Consul agent fleet. We were upgrading the Consul agent, which runs on each instance...
trigger.description: Slack was performing a percentage-based rollout of a Consul agent upgrade, which involved sequential restarts of the Consul agent across the fleet, including on memcached hosts.

change_at.quote: The PBR step on February 22 updated Consul on 25% of the fleet.

mechanism.label: cascading_overload
mechanism.quote: we hit a tipping point and entered a cascading failure scenario as we hit peak traffic for the day
mechanism.description: Consul agent restarts caused Mcrib to churn the memcached cache ring (flushing and replacing nodes), dropping cache hit rates; combined with an inefficient scatter query that had to hit every shard of a Vitess keyspace on any cache miss, this overwhelmed the database and produced a self-sustaining cascading failure that broke client boot for many users.

detected_at.quote: Just after 6 a.m. Pacific Time, a number of things happened almost simultaneously: we began to receive user tickets about problems connecting to Slack, some internal users experienced problems using Slack, and a number of our engineering teams received pages or alerts about problems.

record.title: Roblox Return to Service  | Roblox
record.summary: Roblox experienced a 73-hour outage starting October 28, 2021, caused by enabling a Consul streaming feature on a traffic-routing service under high load, which triggered severe lock contention, combined with a pathological BoltDB freelist performance issue used by Consul for Raft logs. A single shared Consul cluster amplified the impact, and circular telemetry dependencies hampered diagnosis. The team went through multiple failed diagnosis and recovery attempts before disabling streaming and working around slow leaders, then rebuilt caches and gradually restored player access.

change_at.quote: On October 27th at 14:00, one day before the outage, we enabled this feature on a backend service that is responsible for traffic routing.

mechanism.label: lock_contention
mechanism.quote: The majority of time was spent in kernel spin locks via the Streaming subscription code path.
mechanism.description: Under high read and write load, the Consul streaming feature's use of Go channels caused severe contention/blocking, compounded by a BoltDB freelist maintenance issue causing slow writes and unhealthy leaders.

record.title: February 8th, 2019 - Prow responding slow & Partial outage
record.summary: A Prow deploy from an auto-generated bump PR caused a client refactor bug to surface: the build-cluster secret's literal 'default' cluster alias was not respected, so Prow scheduled workloads onto the service cluster instead of the build cluster. This caused jobs to fail to start (missing volumes/credentials) and the service cluster to become overloaded, making all Prow controllers slow and unusable. Engineers rolled back Prow twice, eventually to before the bug was introduced, and a fix PR was merged to prevent the alias override.

record.title: February 8th, 2019 - Prow responding slow & Partial outage
record.summary: An auto-generated Prow bump PR containing a client refactor was merged and deployed on Feb 8, 2019, and the new client code failed to respect a literal 'default' cluster alias defined in the build-cluster secret, causing Prow to schedule most test job workloads onto the service cluster instead of the build cluster. Jobs scheduled on the service cluster could not start due to missing volumes/credentials, and the service cluster became resource-exhausted, making all other Prow controllers extremely slow and largely unusable. Engineers rolled Prow back through several versions, eventually identifying the root cause (an unrespected default cluster alias) with help from an external contributor, applied a targeted fix, cleaned up stuck pods/jobs, and confirmed Prow was healthy again.

document.title: More details about the October 4 outage

record.title: More details about the October 4 outage
record.summary: A routine maintenance command intended to assess global backbone capacity instead took down all backbone connections, disconnecting Facebook's data centers globally; a bug in the audit tool failed to stop the erroneous command. This caused DNS servers to withdraw their BGP advertisements as they appeared unhealthy, making Facebook's services unreachable. Recovery was slowed because internal tools depended on the same downed network, and engineers had to physically access hardened data centers to restore connectivity, after which services were carefully brought back online to avoid a power/traffic surge.

document.title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019

record.title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019
record.summary: On July 2, 2019, Cloudflare deployed a new WAF Managed Rules change containing a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking, which exhausted CPU on every core handling HTTP/HTTPS traffic worldwide. This caused widespread 502 errors for customers globally for 27 minutes. Engineers used a global terminate mechanism to disable the WAF, restoring traffic, and later re-enabled the WAF after fixing the rule. Multiple contributing issues, including a missing CPU-usage protection and access problems during the incident, delayed the response.

record.title: Post-Incident Review on the Atlassian April 2022 outage - Inside Atlassian
record.summary: On April 5, 2022, an internal engineering script intended to delete a legacy 'Insight - Asset Management' app instead deleted 883 entire customer sites (775 customers) due to a communication gap that provided site IDs instead of app IDs, combined with an API that lacked warnings distinguishing site vs app deletion. Restoration required building new multi-site, multi-product recovery automation, with some customers restored within days and all sites restored by April 18, 2022. The incident also deleted customer contact information, hampering support and communications.

document.title: Our October 20 Service Disruption: What Happened, What We Learned and How We’re Improving | LaunchDarkly

record.title: Our October 20 Service Disruption: What Happened, What We Learned and How We’re Improving | LaunchDarkly
record.summary: On October 20, 2025, LaunchDarkly suffered a widespread service disruption in two phases. The first phase was caused by a major AWS us-east-1 outage that degraded EC2, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Route 53, affecting LaunchDarkly's web app, API, flag delivery, and event ingestion. A second phase began when an internal change intended to reduce load reverted flag delivery to a legacy routing path with cold caches, causing excessive SDK retries that overwhelmed the streaming service and load balancer, compounded by ongoing EC2 provisioning issues preventing scale-out. Full recovery of streaming occurred by 12:05 AM PT on October 21, with the incident resolved on the status page at 2:45 AM PT.

mechanism.label: unsafe_failover
mechanism.quote: we reverted to a legacy routing path with cold caches. This caused excessive retries from SDKs. The resulting traffic overwhelmed the streaming service and its load balancer
mechanism.description: The system reverted to a legacy routing path with cold caches, which could not handle the resulting load, causing excessive SDK retries that overwhelmed the streaming service and load balancer.

resolved_at.quote: by 2:45 AM, we resolved the public incident on our status page

blast_radius.qualitative: Widespread disruption to feature flag management, delivery, guarded releases, observability, experimentation, analytics products, and other data features, with US commercial environment most affected.

Scaled out load balancers in all regions for the flag delivery network.
Accelerating migration to a new fault-tolerant delivery architecture.
SDKs and Relay Proxy will support automatic failover from streaming to polling mode.
Relocating disaster recovery orchestration systems out of us-east-1.
Investigating multi-region improvements across critical services and vendor services.
Improving quarterly DR testing to incorporate more gameday realism.
Updating communications process to surface customer workarounds earlier.

contributing_factors.text: Infrastructure couldn't scale out due to ongoing EC2 provisioning issues, extending the outage.
The AWS us-east-1 outage degraded EC2, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Route 53's control plane, causing the initial widespread failure.

document.title: Incident Review: Shepherd Cache Delays

record.title: Incident Review: Shepherd Cache Delays
record.summary: On September 8th, 2022, Honeycomb's ingest system experienced a repeating 'shark fin' failure pattern lasting over eight hours, caused by Shepherd hosts running out of memory and crashing, with cascading crashes in the Refinery cluster. Engineers eventually found that a table-wide lock in Shepherd's in-memory schema cache caused requests to pile up when the cache was updated. The team fixed the issue by reducing cache contention and pre-filling the cache before Shepherd hosts accepted traffic, which stabilized ingest, connection pools, Kafka, and Shepherd, though the ultimate trigger for the initial instability was never identified.

mechanism.label: lock_contention
mechanism.quote: And the lock was table-wide. When a missing entry was backfilled, the cache could cause unrelated requests to pile up.
mechanism.description: A table-wide lock acquired on every Shepherd schema cache update caused unrelated requests to pile up when a missing cache entry was backfilled.

mitigations.text: Applied more aggressive sampling in Refinery to reduce data volume
Scaled Shepherd hosts up vertically to reduce their number
Pinned build versions to prevent deployments from triggering issues
Forced a scale-down of Shepherd hosts (later abandoned due to autoscaler interference)
Applied a fix reducing contention on the cache hot path and pre-filling the cache before Shepherd hosts accept traffic
Added more hosts to the Refinery pool to sustain heavier load from Shepherd

document.title: Intermittent downtime from repeated crashes | Blog | incident.io

record.title: Intermittent downtime from repeated crashes | Blog | incident.io
record.summary: On 18th November 2022, incident.io's app crashed repeatedly (H10 errors) after processing a bad Pub/Sub event that triggered an unhandled panic in a goroutine spawned by the Pub/Sub client library, which was not caught by the app's recover() handlers. The team manually restarted dynos and eventually purged the offending subscriptions, stopping the crash loop after 32 minutes (13 minutes of actual downtime). They then deployed a fix to catch panics in nested goroutines and separated the app into distinct web/worker/cron dynos to prevent similar cross-impact in the future.

trigger.label: content_update
trigger.quote: The subscription responsible was used for generating a welcome message whenever people first enter an incident channel.
trigger.description: A particular async Pub/Sub message (used to generate welcome messages) triggered code that failed for a small subset of customers, repeatedly crashing the app when redelivered.

mechanism.label: software_defect
mechanism.quote: In Go, goroutines have no meaningful links back to their parent. If your child goroutine panics, it won’t benefit from the parent goroutine having applied a recover: it’s an unhandled panic, and your whole app would crash.
mechanism.description: A goroutine spawned internally by the Pub/Sub client library's Receive method panicked while processing a bad message, and this panic was unhandled because the app's recover() was only applied to the parent goroutine, crashing the whole app.

detected_at.quote: Initial crash

mitigations.text: Manually rebooted Heroku dynos to bring the app back up
Purged GCP Pub/Sub subscriptions with unacked messages from around the crash time
Disabled non-critical async features (e.g. incident nudges) to prioritize core functionality

resolved_at.quote: Deploy split of web, worker and cron into different dynos

blast_radius.qualitative: 13 minutes of downtime over a period of 32 minutes

quantitative.quote: we experienced 13 minutes of downtime over a period of 32 minutes
over a period of 32 minutes from 15:40 to 16:12 GMT

mitigated_at.quote: App stops crashing

remediations.text: Deployed fix to add recover() handling for panics in goroutines spawned by the Pub/Sub client's Receive method
Physically split the app into separate web, worker and cron dynos on Heroku

record.detection_quote: our on-call engineer was paged due to an "H10 - App crashed" error code from Heroku

contributing_factors.text: Go's panic behavior prints the stacktrace of every goroutine (~300), causing Heroku to buffer and drop log lines, preventing visibility into the crashing stacktrace.
Because Go exits immediately on unhandled panic, even panic-handled components like Sentry error reporting were terminated, preventing crash inspection in the exception tracker.
Heroku's rate limiting of logs also impacted logs just prior to a crash, preventing visibility into which event was being processed.

document.title: One, Two, Skip a Few... | Blog | incident.io

record.title: One, Two, Skip a Few... | Blog | incident.io
record.summary: incident.io customers noticed their incident IDs jumping unexpectedly, e.g. by exactly 32. Investigation revealed Postgres pre-allocates and logs 32 sequence values in advance, and follower nodes assume all pre-allocated values were used. A recent database upgrade involved promoting a follower to primary, causing sequences to jump forward by up to 32 values. No data was lost, but customer-visible incident numbering appeared inconsistent.

trigger.label: database_failover
trigger.quote: we had upgraded our database recently, which involves spinning up a follower, then promoting it to be the primary.
trigger.description: A database upgrade involved promoting a follower node to primary, causing sequences to jump forward by up to 32 values.

mechanism.label: consistency_anomaly
mechanism.quote: follower nodes will see the state "that would prevail on the primary if it were to crash", which as above, is likely to be up to 32 ahead of the current sequence value.
mechanism.description: Postgres pre-allocates and WAL-logs sequence values in batches of 32; a promoted follower assumes all pre-allocated values were used, causing sequence values to skip ahead inconsistently with actual usage.

blast_radius.qualitative: No data was lost or misattributed, but customer incident numbering appeared to jump unexpectedly.

quantitative.quote: One customer with 20 incidents was reporting that we'd labelled their most recent incident as #INC-52
seen their incident IDs jump from #INC-7 to #INC-39

remediations.text: Moved to a new approach using MAX(external_id)+1 in a before-insert trigger instead of Postgres sequences, to enforce strictly incrementing-by-1 IDs.

record.detection_quote: we started getting strange reports from some customers of incident.io.

contributing_factors.text: Postgres pre-logs sequence fetches in batches of 32 to avoid excessive WAL writes, which can cause skipped values on crash or promotion.

record.title: An Outage Post-Mortem for August 22nd – what went wrong?
record.summary: Buildkite downgraded its production RDS PostgreSQL database and moved to a centralized pgbouncer to cut AWS costs, without adequate load testing. Under Monday US peak load the new database's CPU maxed out, causing health checks to fail and a cascade of ELB server removals and failed replacements due to a broken self-deploy mechanism. A misconfigured PagerDuty notification setting meant on-call staff were not woken up, delaying response by ~4 hours, and AWS IAM/EC2 limit issues further hampered recovery efforts before the database was upgraded and service restored.

trigger.label: config_change
trigger.quote: We looked at some graphs and decided to downgrade to a more affordable r3.2xlarge Multi-AZ RDS PostgreSQL instance.
trigger.description: Buildkite downgraded its production RDS PostgreSQL instance and moved to a centralized pgbouncer to reduce AWS costs, without adequate load testing.

mechanism.label: cascading_overload
mechanism.quote: These performance problems started a cascade of other issues.
mechanism.description: The downgraded database couldn't handle peak load, causing CPU exhaustion that triggered failing health checks, ELB server removals, and a cascade of new servers failing to come online.

detected_at.quote: We woke up at 21:00 UTC almost 4 hours after we went offline

mitigations.text: Made temporary fixes to bring buildkite.com back online
Stole servers from the Agent API ELB and added them to the dashboard ELB
Upgraded the database to a larger instance type
Removed the centralized pgbouncer and reverted to per-host pgbouncer
Locked Auto Scaling Groups to EC2 health checks and locked in desired counts

resolved_at.quote: We finally recovered at 23:10 UTC

blast_radius.qualitative: No one was able to login, view build logs or read documentation, though builds continued running.

impact_start.quote: On the 22nd of August 2016 at 17:21 UTC, Buildkite suffered a severe unplanned outage.

mitigated_at.quote: at 22:28 UTC we made some temporary fixes to get buildkite.com back online

remediations.text: Switched health check to only verify app connectivity, not database
Considering an additional Pingdom-based health check that verifies database connectivity
Switched to storing latest deployed revision as a file on S3 for self-deploy instead of a live endpoint
Ensure all on-call team members have correct PagerDuty and iPhone settings, with manual verification
Investigate triggering company-wide PagerDuty tests regularly
Requesting PagerDuty call on-call members when they go on-call, or require 'Immediately phone' rule
Plan to do load testing after significant infrastructure changes
Learned about and plan to use AWS 'Suspend and Resume Auto Scaling Processes' feature

record.detection_quote: We woke up at 21:00 UTC almost 4 hours after we went offline to see our phones full of emails, tweets and Slack messages letting us know Buildkite was down.
record.time_to_detect_text: almost 4 hours after we went offline

contributing_factors.text: Health check endpoints checked database connectivity, causing all servers to fail out of the ELB when the database was unhealthy.
New servers self-deployed via a version endpoint that only worked when buildkite.com was online, causing them to run stale code referencing a decommissioned database shard.
PagerDuty 'Immediately phone me' notification rule was dropped and phones were on silent, so on-call staff were not woken up.
AWS IAM issues and EC2 request limits prevented the team from making console changes and launching new servers during recovery.

document.title: I deleted the production database by accident 💥

record.title: I deleted the production database by accident 💥
record.summary: The developer ran a local database reset function intending to wipe and recreate a local development database, but due to an incorrect environment variable setting the function connected to and wiped the production database instead. Over 300,000 scoreboards were deleted, and the site was put into maintenance mode while a backup was restored. About 30 minutes later the site was back online, but roughly 7 hours of data (scores/scoreboards created between 15:47 CET and 23:21 CET) was permanently lost.

trigger.quote: The function that wiped the database was written to delete the local database and create tables from scratch. However, it connected to the production database and wiped it due to a misconfiguration.
trigger.description: The developer ran a database reset function intended for local use, which due to a misconfigured environment variable connected to and wiped the production database.

mechanism.description: A function intended to drop and recreate local database tables was accidentally run against the production database, deleting all production data.

mitigations.text: Took the website into maintenance mode
Restored a backup from DigitalOcean's automatic daily backups

resolved_at.quote: At around 11:15pm CET, 30 minutes after the disaster, I went back online

record.title: Tarsnap outage 2016-07-24 10:15:19--11:40:04
record.summary: Starting around June 30th 2016, Tarsnap's servers saw a sharp increase in correlated timeout failures from Amazon S3, causing a background block-freeing job to repeatedly abort and its log of freed blocks to grow unbounded. On 2016-07-24 at 10:15:19 UTC this log filled the filesystem, causing writes to fail and triggering an automatic shutdown of all Tarsnap service code as a safety measure. Monitoring alerted the operator via text and phone, but he slept through the first alerts; after waking to a second phone call, he diagnosed the issue, deleted the runaway log file, and restarted the service, restoring normal operation by 11:40:04 UTC, 85 minutes after the outage began.

trigger.label: external_service_degradation
trigger.quote: The Tarsnap server starts to experience an increase in correlated timeout failures from Amazon S3.
trigger.description: An unexplained change in Amazon S3 behaviour caused a sharp rise in requests exhausting all retries, leading to repeated failures of a background block-freeing job.

mechanism.label: resource_exhaustion
mechanism.quote: The log of blocks being freed, which now lists many blocks over a hundred times each, fills the filesystem on which it is stored.
mechanism.description: A log file recording freed S3 blocks grew unbounded due to repeated job aborts, filling the filesystem and causing other writes to fail, which triggered a full service shutdown.

detected_at.quote: Tarsnap's monitoring systems determine that the Tarsnap service is not operating properly, and send me a text message.

mitigations.text: Operator deleted the runaway log file that had filled the filesystem.
Restarted the aborted server code and confirmed normal operation.

resolved_at.quote: Tarsnap monitoring shows everything functioning normally.

blast_radius.qualitative: Tarsnap service was fully offline for storing and retrieving archives for 85 minutes; no customer data was lost.

quantitative.quote: for a period of 85 minutes
142 times over the following week: Writes to Amazon S3 fail repeatedly, causing the aforementioned background job to abort.
quantitative.metric: background job restarts due to S3 write failures

quantitative.quote: I have credited Tarsnap users' accounts with 2 days of storage costs due to this 85 minute outage.

impact_start.quote: At approximately 2016-07-24 10:15:19 UTC, the Tarsnap service went offline

mitigated_at.quote: I restart the server code which had aborted, and confirm that it's all working properly again.

remediations.text: Set monitoring to phone once an hour to ensure operator is woken.
Consider better internal monitoring of metrics like filesystem free space, weighing security tradeoffs before implementation.
Commit to investigating anomalous behaviour in the future even if believed harmless.

record.detection_quote: Tarsnap's monitoring systems determine that the Tarsnap service is not operating properly, and send me a text message.

contributing_factors.text: Inappropriate handling of repeated S3 failures resulted in runaway disk space consumption.
A lack of sufficient internal monitoring allowed the issue to go undetected until it became critical.
The operator slept through the first text message and phone call, extending the outage roughly threefold.
Anomalous S3 retry failures were noticed earlier in July but not investigated because they seemed harmless.

document.title: Outage report 7 July 2020

record.title: Outage report 7 July 2020
record.summary: On 7 July 2020 at 16:06 UTC, an EBS storage volume attached to file server livefile1 failed with multiple component failures, causing filesystem access to block and time out. This caused PythonAnywhere's own site to slow down and error, and websites, scheduled tasks and always-on tasks for accounts hosted on livefile1 to go down, with effects spreading to other hosted sites via blocked worker processes. Engineers rebuilt the file server's volumes from backup snapshots rather than promoting the backup server, and performed a rolling reboot; the site was fully back to normal by 21:24 UTC, with volumes fully warmed up by 23:50 UTC.

mechanism.label: hardware_data_loss
mechanism.quote: an EBS volume had multiple component failures, essentially meaning that a complete redundant array of disks stopped working
mechanism.description: An EBS storage volume attached to file server livefile1 suffered multiple component failures, causing the underlying redundant disk array to stop working.

detected_at.quote: Our monitoring system notified our support team of a number of issues spread across multiple machines in our cluster.

mitigations.text: Rebooted and re-provisioned the failed file server onto new hardware
Rebuilt file server volumes from backup server snapshots and resynced
Performed a rolling reboot of servers accessing livefile1
Warmed up new volumes via various tricks in parallel with getting sites running faster

resolved_at.quote: The new volumes were fully warmed up, and file access was completely back to normal.

blast_radius.qualitative: Affected pretty much everyone who uses the site at some point, though only accounts on livefile1 (20% of users) had prolonged outages.

quantitative.quote: 80% of users are stored on other file servers.

impact_start.quote: At 16:06 UTC on 7 July 2020, a storage volume failure on one of our storage servers caused a number of outages

mitigated_at.quote: All sites were up and running again. ... we tweeted that the incident was over.

remediations.text: Investigate ways to reduce storage volume failure further, e.g. using fewer volumes per storage server
Work on limiting the scope of an outage so that a single file server failure only affects accounts stored on it
Develop a fully tested script to rebuild a file server's volumes from backups
Investigate reducing or eliminating the need for a rolling reboot of the cluster
Investigate warming up volumes ahead of time by using old backup volumes with unwarmed snapshots on the backup server

record.detection_quote: Our monitoring system notified our support team of a number of issues spread across multiple machines in our cluster.

contributing_factors.text: Identifying the underlying cause took over an hour because the team lacked the admin tooling AWS support had.
The scripts for rebuilding a file server's volumes from backup were assembled in realtime rather than pre-built, taking almost an hour.
The rolling reboot of the cluster to restore access affected accounts on other, unaffected file servers.
New volumes created from snapshots were unwarmed and slow, causing continued slowness after recovery.
livefile1 only held a portion of user data, but the outage affected nearly everyone due to shared worker processes blocking on it.

document.title: Incident 2023-12-04: Data leak and loss in some free tier databases

record.title: Incident 2023-12-04: Data leak and loss in some free tier databases
record.summary: A migration bug introduced on November 20th caused some free-tier databases to be configured with an empty backup identifier, making them share a backup storage location. When those databases failed to scale back up, on December 1st internal recreation procedures restored them from the shared null-ID backup, causing data leakage across databases and eventual loss of recent writes. The issue was reported on December 4th and fixed the same day by re-running the migration correctly and restoring from the correct December 1st backups, discarding any writes made after that date.

trigger.label: code_deploy
trigger.quote: A change that made possible for the empty backup identifier to be used was made to the system on November 20th.
trigger.description: A migration deployed around November 20th contained a bug that caused some databases to be assigned an empty/shared backup identifier.

change_at.quote: A change that made possible for the empty backup identifier to be used was made to the system on November 20th.

mechanism.label: consistency_anomaly
mechanism.quote: Effectively, the databases in that small set were now sharing a backup storage bucket.
mechanism.description: Affected databases shared a single backup storage location due to an empty backup ID, causing cross-database data leakage and loss upon recreation from that shared backup.

detected_at.quote: This was noticed and reported on December 4th 8:10 AM UTC

mitigations.text: Re-ran the migration with correct parameters and recreated affected databases from their December 1st backup with correct backup ID, discarding writes after that point.

resolved_at.quote: fixed on December 4th 9:17 AM UTC

blast_radius.qualitative: 0.07% of databases under management were incorrectly configured with an empty backup identifier, which caused a data leak.

quantitative.quote: 0.07% of databases under management were incorrectly configured with an empty backup identifier

impact_start.quote: On December 1st, internal procedures led to those backups being used to recreate the databases.

mitigated_at.quote: fixed on December 4th 9:17 AM UTC

remediations.text: Add additional internal checks from control plane and data plane to ensure backups are for the correct database, improving data isolation in backups.
Improve ability to check for faulty configuration and to self-heal or notify a team member.
Improve deployment methods to prevent migrations from breaking backup IDs.
Add better mechanisms for being notified of security incidents via twitter or email.

record.detection_quote: Thanks to Schlez for notifying us and allowing us to get to a solution quickly.

contributing_factors.text: Free tier databases scale to zero and are recreated from S3 backups when fly.io cannot restore the process due to lack of host resources.

document.title: Knightmare: A DevOps Cautionary Tale

record.title: Knightmare: A DevOps Cautionary Tale
record.summary: Knight Capital deployed updated SMARS trading software to seven of eight servers, leaving old 'Power Peg' code active on the eighth due to an incomplete manual deployment. When markets opened on August 1, 2012, orders routed to the eighth server activated the dormant Power Peg code, which lacked tracking of parent order fulfillment and generated a flood of uncontrolled child orders. Over 45 minutes, Knight's systems executed millions of erroneous trades, and confused responders made things worse by removing the correctly-deployed code, amplifying the problem across all servers. The resulting $460 million loss left Knight Capital insolvent within 45 minutes.

trigger.label: code_deploy
trigger.quote: one of Knight’s technicians did not copy the new code to one of the eight SMARS computer servers
trigger.description: Knight manually deployed updated SMARS code to eight servers between July 27-31, 2012, but one technician failed to copy the new code to the eighth server.

change_at.quote: Between July 27, 2012 and July 31, 2012 Knight manually deployed the new software to a limited number of servers per day

mechanism.label: software_defect
mechanism.quote: the Power Peg functionality began routing child orders for execution, but wasn’t tracking the amount of shares against the parent order – somewhat like an endless loop
mechanism.description: The repurposed flag reactivated dormant Power Peg code on the eighth server, which routed child orders without tracking fulfillment against the parent order, causing runaway order generation.

detected_at.quote: When the market opened at 9:30 AM people quickly knew something was wrong.

mitigations.text: Attempted to uninstall the newly deployed code from servers, mistakenly removing the correctly working code instead of the broken Power Peg code, which worsened the issue.
Eventually stopped the system after 45 minutes of trading.

blast_radius.qualitative: Knight's executions constituted more than 50% of trading volume during the first 45 minutes, driving some stocks up over 10% in value, and the company was rendered insolvent.

quantitative.quote: the Power Peg code received and processed 212 parent orders
resulting in 4 million transactions against 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares

for more than 397 million shares

$3.15 billion net short positions in 74 stocks

record.title: Knightmare: A DevOps Cautionary Tale
record.summary: Knight Capital updated its SMARS trading router to replace old, unused 'Power Peg' code with new Retail Liquidity Program functionality, repurposing an old flag. During manual deployment across eight servers, one technician failed to deploy the new code to one server, leaving the dormant Power Peg code active there. document.title: Billing Incident Post-Mortem: Breakdown, Analysis and Root Cause

record.title: Billing Incident Post-Mortem: Breakdown, Analysis and Root Cause
record.summary: On July 18, 2013, Twilio's billing system experienced a loss of network connectivity between billing redis-slaves and the redis-master, causing all slaves to reconnect and request full sync simultaneously and overloading the master. On-call engineers misdiagnosed the issue and restarted redis-master, which booted with an incorrect configuration, dropped all balance data, and came up read-only as a slave of itself. With zero balances and read-only mode, the billing system repeatedly attempted credit card recharges, causing erroneous charges and account suspensions affecting 1.4% of customers. Twilio restored balances from a separate relational datastore, refunded customers, and fully restored service by July 20.

mechanism.description: Incorrect config caused redis-master to lose balance data and boot read-only as a slave of itself, leaving billing balances inconsistent with actual state and triggering repeated erroneous recharges.

document.title: Retrospective and Technical Details on the recent Firefox Outage – Mozilla Hacks - the Web developer blog

record.title: Retrospective and Technical Details on the recent Firefox Outage – Mozilla Hacks - the Web developer blog
record.summary: On January 13th 2022, GCP silently changed its load balancer defaults to enable HTTP/3, causing Firefox's Telemetry service connections to use HTTP/3 instead of HTTP/2. A case-sensitivity mismatch between the viaduct library (which lower-cases headers) and Necko's HTTP/3 code (which checks Content-Length case-sensitively) caused the header to be missed, leaving the request body unsent. This caused an infinite loop on Firefox's single socket thread, blocking all network communication and making the browser unresponsive worldwide for close to two hours.

trigger.label: external_service_degradation
trigger.quote: on January 13, 2022 at 07:28 UTC, GCP deployed an unannounced change to make HTTP/3 the default
trigger.description: GCP deployed an unannounced change making HTTP/3 the default for load balancers, causing Telemetry connections to switch from HTTP/2 to HTTP/3.

change_at.quote: on January 13, 2022 at 07:28 UTC, GCP deployed an unannounced change to make HTTP/3 the default

mechanism.label: other
mechanism.quote: this unexpected state caused the code to loop indefinitely rather than returning an error
mechanism.description: A case-sensitivity mismatch between viaduct's lower-cased headers and Necko's case-sensitive HTTP/3 header check caused the Content-Length header to be missed, leading to an infinite loop on the socket thread that blocked all network communication.

mitigations.text: Disabled HTTP/3 explicitly on GCP load balancers.

blast_radius.qualitative: Firefox became unusable for close to two hours for users worldwide.

quantitative.quote: Backlog of pending crash reports building up and reaching close to 300K unprocessed reports.

impact_start.quote: on January 13, 2022 at 07:28 UTC, GCP deployed an unannounced change to make HTTP/3 the default

mitigated_at.quote: We disabled HTTP/3 explicitly on GCP at 09:12 UTC.

remediations.text: Working with GCP to improve announcement of such changes.
Reviewing all service configurations to avoid similar 'Automatic (default)' mistakes.
Plan to run more system tests with different HTTP versions and networking layers.
Investigating action points to make the browser more resilient and improve incident response speed.

record.detection_quote: Shortly after, we noticed a spike in crashes being reported through our crash reporter and also received several reports from inside and outside of Mozilla describing a hang of the browser.

contributing_factors.text: GCP's deployment of HTTP/3 as default was unannounced.
Mozilla's load balancer setting of 'Automatic (default)' allowed the deployment to take place automatically instead of an explicit choice.
The particular combination of HTTP/3 and viaduct on Firefox Desktop was not covered in the continuous integration system.

record.title: Postmortem for Malicious Packages Published on July 12th, 2018 - ESLint - Pluggable JavaScript Linter
record.summary: On July 12th, 2018, an attacker compromised the npm account of an ESLint maintainer, who had reused their password and lacked two-factor authentication, and published malicious versions of eslint-scope and eslint-config-eslint to npm. The malicious packages contained a postinstall script that downloaded and executed code from pastebin.com to exfiltrate users' .npmrc authentication tokens. The malicious versions were unpublished, the pastebin link was taken down, and npm revoked all access tokens issued before the compromise.

trigger.quote: an attacker compromised the npm account of an ESLint maintainer and published malicious versions
trigger.description: An attacker compromised the npm account of an ESLint maintainer using a reused, breached password, with no two-factor authentication enabled.

mechanism.label: security_compromise
mechanism.quote: the malicious packages downloaded and executed code from pastebin.com which sent the contents of the user's .npmrc file to the attacker
mechanism.description: Using the compromised account, the attacker published malicious package versions containing a postinstall script that exfiltrated npm authentication tokens via pastebin.com.

detected_at.quote: 2018-07-12 11:17 UTC: A user posted eslint/eslint-scope#39, notifying the ESLint team of the issue.

mitigations.text: Unpublished eslint-config-eslint@5.0.2
pastebin.com link taken down
npm unpublished eslint-scope@3.7.2
ESLint published eslint-scope@3.7.3 with code from 3.7.1 so caches could pick up the new version

Recommend package maintainers enable npm two-factor authentication

document.title: March 26th, 2019 Boskos Outage

record.title: March 26th, 2019 Boskos Outage
record.summary: A hidden bug introduced in a December 2018 commit prevented Boskos from starting up, but went unnoticed because a StatefulSet spec update in March 2019 did not actually replace the running pod. When the node hosting the only Boskos pod was drained during a Kubernetes 1.11-to-1.13 cluster upgrade, the pod was rescheduled and picked up the buggy image, causing Boskos to crash-loop. All jobs requiring GCP projects from Boskos, including a required kubernetes/kubernetes PR check, failed for over nine hours while on-call was asleep, until the bug was found and a fixed image deployed.

trigger.quote: At 23:04 the node running the only Boskos pod was drained to be replaced with a 1.13 node, and boskos was moved to a new node.

change_at.quote: [03-26 23:04] The node hosting boskos is drained. The replacement pod is stuck in a crash loop.

mechanism.label: software_defect
mechanism.quote: A bug was introduced in a commit that landed in December last year, that when deployed would cause Boskos to be unable to start up.
mechanism.description: A bug introduced in a December commit prevented Boskos from starting up (failing to create its CRD client) once it was actually deployed, causing a crash loop.

detected_at.quote: [03-26 02:50] The outage is reported on GitHub by @mborsz

mitigations.text: A new fixed image was built and deployed, allowing Boskos to recover immediately.

resolved_at.quote: [03-26 08:10] @Katharine successfully deploys a fixed Boskos (**outage ends**)

Automate Boskos deploys
Improve alerting around boskos status

record.detection_quote: Users reported issues at 02:50 (via GitHub), 05:16 and 06:27 (both via Slack).

contributing_factors.text: The Boskos StatefulSet was not configured to trigger pod updates when the spec changed, so the buggy image update went unnoticed for a week.
The December bug was never tested before being merged.
Boskos deployments are handled manually rather than automated like most of Prow, increasing room for error.
No alerting caught the outage even though monitoring showed the failure clearly.

document.title: May 30th, 2019 Prow Flakiness

record.title: May 30th, 2019 Prow Flakiness
record.summary: Increasing test load over time led to increased I/O usage on the k8s-prow-build cluster, and a spike in usage around the Kubernetes 1.15 code freeze caused nodes to hit hard GCP IOPS throttling limits. This throttling caused I/O operations to take so long that nodes experienced kernel panics and kubelet crashes, leading to widespread test failures, missing artifacts, and a stalled merge queue. The team requested additional disk quota and migrated the cluster from 250GB to 500GB disks to increase available IOPS, resolving the issue after several hours.

mechanism.quote: a spike in usage lead to hitting hard throttling limits, causing I/O operations to take so long that nodes experienced kernel panics and test code wildly misbehaved.

record.title: May 30th, 2019 Prow Flakiness
record.summary: Increasing test load on the k8s-prow-build cluster led to a spike in disk I/O usage around the Kubernetes 1.15 code freeze, hitting GCP's hard IOPS throttling limits. This caused I/O operations to take so long that nodes experienced kernel panics and test pods misbehaved, resulting in widespread test failures, missing artifacts, and a stalled merge queue. The team resolved it by migrating the cluster from 250GB to 500GB disks, which provided more IOPS.

trigger.label: traffic_spike
trigger.quote: In the run-up to the Kubernetes 1.15 code freeze, a spike in usage lead to hitting hard throttling limits
trigger.description: A spike in test load in the run-up to the Kubernetes 1.15 code freeze caused I/O usage to exceed GCP's hard IOPS throttling limits.

mechanism.label: resource_exhaustion
mechanism.quote: a spike in usage lead to hitting hard throttling limits, causing I/O operations to take so long that nodes experienced kernel panics and test code wildly misbehaved
mechanism.description: Nodes exhausted their GCP-allotted IOPS quota, causing I/O operations to take so long that nodes suffered kernel panics and pods misbehaved.

detected_at.quote: @cblecker reports on Slack that something is wrong with Prow

mitigations.text: Requested and received quota for additional disk space and migrated the cluster to 500 GB disks instead of 250 GB disks.
Brought up 55 nodes with 500 GB disks to relieve pressure.
Gradually migrated existing nodes to the 500GB node pool.

resolved_at.quote: Prow is once again merging at its usual rate

blast_radius.qualitative: Many tests failing in surprising ways, jobs aborted, artifacts not uploaded, merge queue stalled for many hours, 1.15 code freeze slipped a day.

quantitative.quote: At peak, 60 PRs were stuck in the merge queue
we've managed to exhaust our IOPS quota... by a factor of two

impact_start.quote: [???] IOPS reached a critical point such that cluster availability began degrading

mitigated_at.quote: @BenTheElder completes the migration to the new node pool, all nodes now have 500 GB disks

remediations.text: Create and/or fix monitoring so that when tide stops doing things the oncall gets paged (#12829)
Establish a process and guidelines for adding new members to the oncall rotation so they are not thrown in the deep end without preparation or extra support.

record.detection_quote: Multiple users reported jobs that were reported to GitHub as having failed, but which upon checking the job status actually appeared to still be running.

contributing_factors.text: Prow metrics were not being recorded in the runup to the incident, making it difficult to figure out what was going on.
Alerting for these failures either does not exist or does not work.
Once the cause had been determined and a fix devised, nothing was done for another two hours.
Due to an unrelated monitoring failure, most prow/tide monitoring for the week leading to this incident is permanently lost, making it difficult to establish how long the cluster was faulty.

record.title: AGILE in Financial Services
record.summary: A storage controller in King's College London's HP 3PAR storage system at the Strand Data Centre failed on 17 October 2016; when HP engineers replaced the component, a firmware flaw prevented the system from returning online and multiple disks failed, causing complete data loss on the device. Recovery relied on backup systems, but tape and secondary backups had not been reliably maintained or tested, so some data (e.g. Admissions) could not be fully recovered. A business continuity process was invoked and services were progressively restored over several weeks, with full handover to operations teams by late November 2016.

trigger.label: infrastructure_maintenance
trigger.quote: HP hardware engineers then arrived on site to replace the component that had failed.
trigger.description: HP hardware engineers replaced a failed storage controller in the Strand HP 3PAR system, which triggered a firmware flaw that prevented normal recovery.

change_at.quote: On the 17th October 2016 one of the four controllers within the principal HP storage system located in the Strand Data Centre failed.

mechanism.label: software_defect
mechanism.quote: the inability of the storage system to return to service after the defective hardware was replaced was due to a flaw in the firmware responsible for keeping the hardware controllers functional
mechanism.description: A flaw in the HP storage controller firmware prevented the system from returning to service after the failed controller was replaced, causing the system to go offline and disks to fail, resulting in complete data loss.

detected_at.quote: At this point what had been a routine incident with no impact to users was escalated to senior management in the IT team.

mitigations.text: A pre-documented business continuity process was instigated to establish a cross-functional response team to co-ordinate incident resolution and service recovery.
Priority services were identified and restored in stages, including shared drive and IOPPN data recovery.
Additional backups from a retired backup device were used to restore some data.

resolved_at.quote: IT P1 Closed?

blast_radius.qualitative: The outage had catastrophic impact on the College, resulting in permanent loss of some data despite significant effort to recreate it.

impact_start.quote: Routine HW failure

mitigated_at.quote: All main services restored; J: Drive restored

remediations.text: Backup coverage reviewed and tape library capacity increased.
Daily Service Review update coverage revised and communicated so all team members understand business significance.
All systems to be subject to an annual recovery test to verify backup and recovery capability.
Migrated more systems to a new distributed backup system (Veeam) to relieve load on legacy tape backup.
Develop and communicate clear data storage policies and guidance, and initiate a college-wide culture change programme.
Review and adjust wider College IT governance structure, delegating decisions based on complexity, scale and investment.

record.detection_quote: the system went offline and simultaneously many of the storage disks within it started failing leading to a complete loss of data. At this point what had been a routine incident with no impact to users was escalated to senior management in the IT team.

contributing_factors.text: The IT team did not fully understand the importance of tape backups and did not follow backup procedures completely.
Some data was consciously never backed up on tape due to capacity constraints, and this was not communicated to the College.
Backup performance had never been tested, making recovery time estimates unreliable.
HP had issued an updated firmware version weeks before the incident that would have allowed the replacement without outage, but the IT team had not applied it.
Daily Service Review updates on backup status were reported incorrectly, masking repeated backup failures.
The College's support package with HP did not include risk assessment and change management advice available in HP's newer 'enhanced support' option.

document.title: Boeing_737-8K5_G-TWAG_04-21

record.title: Boeing_737-8K5_G-TWAG_04-21
record.summary: A reservation-system upgrade introduced a software flaw that interpreted the title 'Miss' as denoting a child rather than an adult female, causing check-in and load-sheet weight calculations to under-allocate 34 kg per affected passenger. On 21 July 2020, Boeing 737-8K5 G-TAWG departed Birmingham with 38 female passengers misclassified as children, giving a load sheet takeoff weight 1,244 kg below the actual weight. The flight crew noticed a discrepancy but judged it plausible given pandemic-era load variability and proceeded; thrust used was marginally sufficient so safety was not compromised. The operator subsequently introduced manual and automated checks to prevent recurrence.

trigger.label: code_deploy
trigger.quote: prior to the incident flight the reservation system from which the load sheet was produced had been upgraded
trigger.description: The airline's reservation/check-in system, from which load sheets were produced, had been upgraded as part of a wider industry system upgrade prior to the incident flight.

mechanism.label: software_defect
mechanism.quote: There was a fault in the system which, when a female passenger checked in for the flight and used or was given the title 'Miss', caused the system checked her in as a child.
mechanism.description: A programming flaw caused the system to interpret the title 'Miss' as indicating a child rather than an adult female, assigning an incorrect standard weight and producing an inaccurate load sheet.

mitigations.text: A manual solution was identified: a team checked upcoming flight bookings and changed adult females with title 'Miss' to 'Ms'.
The correction process was performed every afternoon and evening for the next day's flights and checked again each morning where possible.
Ground Operations requested check-in staff pay particular attention to female passengers to ensure correct sex/age classification.
Programmers implemented an automated fix that changed titles from Miss to Ms for bookings before check-in.

resolved_at.quote: A more formal system of checks was introduced on 24 July 2020.

blast_radius.qualitative: the safe operation of the aircraft was not compromised

quantitative.quote: with 38 females checked in incorrectly and misidentified as children
quantitative.metric: females checked in incorrectly as children

quantitative.quote: the G-TAWG takeoff mass from the load sheet was 1,244 kg below the actual mass of the aircraft
the number of children shown on the load sheet was higher than expected, at 65, compared to the 29 which were expected on the flight plan
quantitative.metric: children shown on load sheet vs expected

quantitative.quote: Persons on Board: Crew - 6 Passengers - 187

impact_start.quote: 21 July 2020 at 0500 hrs

remediations.text: A member of the Systems team manually checked flights daily to ensure title 'Miss' was amended to 'Ms'.
A secondary check was instigated with the Operations department against booked passenger loads.
A reminder briefing was given to Ground Handling Agents to be alert for adult females showing as Miss or a child.
A formalised procedure for a Customer Care Executive to check bookings was instituted.

record.detection_quote: This was spotted by the flight dispatcher and the operator's systems delivery manager.

contributing_factors.text: No specific test scenarios examining passenger titles were run during User Acceptance Testing, so the flaw was not caught before go-live.
Correction teams did not work over the weekend, and online check-in opened 24 hours before departure on Monday, so incorrectly allocated weights for the incident flight were not corrected in time.
A software 'fix' was being applied to the correction program on 20 July 2020, possibly preventing it from identifying incorrect passenger status before the incident flight.
